Note: SECONDARY: these are Huttenlocher's (1979) observations replotted, not a new measurement; N = 12, as this paper's Table 2 prints. Digitisation: the open circles were pixel-digitised from the embedded page bitmap (1890 x 2850 px, 8-bit grey, PDF p. 4) by Feinberg_etal_1990_Figure1_extract.py (conda env 'python'; pymupdf, numpy, scipy), run 2026-10-31; a second run reports 'snapshot unchanged'. Both axes are SINGLE LINEAR axes; the abscissa is calibrated on the eight printed 5-year ticks and the ordinate on the row centres of the printed tick labels (the ordinate rule is slightly skewed on this scan, so a fixed-column tick scan misses some). Circles are found two ways and merged: the white region each ring encloses, and normalised cross-correlation against a ring template cut from an isolated circle, which recovers rings the fitted gamma curve has broken; marker_detection records which found each point. ESTIMATED ERROR +/- 0.2 x 10^8 synapses/mm3 and +/- 0.2 y. POINTS CONTAINED vs RESOLVED: the panel contains 12 plotted points and all 12 were individually resolved; none was inferred. CROSS-CHECK AGAINST THE PRIMARY SOURCE (built here as Huttenlocher__1979_Figure3): pairing the 12 points by sorted value against the 12 Huttenlocher brains aged <= 32 y, the two digitisations agree to a MEAN of 0.084 and a MAXIMUM of 0.159 x 10^8 synapses/mm3 - within the summed digitisation error of the two figures. The AGES agree to a maximum of 0.85 y for the ten source points that do not fall in one of Huttenlocher's axis breaks, but to 1.44 y over all twelve: the two worst are exactly the two Huttenlocher points that lie inside an axis-break gap. Feinberg's abscissa is a single linear 0-35 y axis, so where the two disagree on an age, this panel is the better reading.
